title: The cathedrals
hookLine: built over generations by people who wouldn't see them finished
last: A KING AT TABLE WITH THE POOR.

lines: A STONE SET, NO ROOF ABOVE.
THE SON LAYS THE NEXT ROW.
cards: A mason sets a block high in a wall, taps it level, and climbs down the scaffold. There's no roof above him yet, and no tower.
His son may lay the next row of stone, and his grandson may be the one who hears the first Mass under the finished vault.
Some great churches rose this way, a few courses at a time, while the people who began them grew old and were buried in the churchyard beside the work.

teach.h: A CATHEDRAL HOLDS A BISHOP'S CHAIR.
teach.b: Start with what makes a church a cathedral. It isn't size. A cathedral is the church that holds a bishop's chair, called the cathedra, the sign of his work of teaching and shepherding.
A small church with that chair is a cathedral; an enormous church without it is not. At the heart of the grandest building in town sits a piece of furniture, and a job. Next, the long build.
Masons, carpenters, glassmakers, donors who paid for one window or gave one season of labor: the building could outlast them all, and their names. Then, the reason.
A psalm in the Douay-Rheims puts it in one line: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it."

teach.h: UNLESS THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.
teach.b: The psalm isn't about masonry, but people raised these churches as if every block were laid for God before it was laid for a town. Finally, the posture.
The letter to the Hebrews remembers the ancestors of faith who died still waiting, "not having received the promises, but beholding them afar off."

That's the cathedral builder's stance. You lay a stone you'll never stand under, and trust someone you'll never meet to finish it. A cathedral is a long sentence, and each generation gets to write a few words of it.

how: Each Catholic diocese has a cathedral where the bishop's chair stands; the bishop presides there at major celebrations, such as the Chrism Mass in Holy Week, and the anniversary of the cathedral's dedication is kept as a feast in the diocese.

o: the church that holds a bishop's chair
the main church of a religious order
any very large and very old church

p: unless the Lord build the house
a small church with a bishop's chair

s: a cathedral is any very large church
a cathedral is the church that holds a bishop's chair. size has nothing to do with it.
Hebrews remembers people who died before receiving the promises
"not having received the promises, but beholding them afar off."
the psalm says builders work in vain unless the Lord builds the house
that is the line the teach quotes from Psalm 126 in the Douay-Rheims.

games.q: you're a mason. the cathedral you're working on won't be finished in your lifetime. what do you do?
o: lay each stone as carefully as if you'd see the roof.
walk away; why build what you'll never use?
cut corners; nobody will know whose stone it was.
games.why: the text that fits this choice is Hebrews: people who kept faith with a promise they saw only afar off.

practice: Choose something small you could begin that will outlast today: a seed in a pot, the first page of a notebook for someone younger, a jar of coins for a cause you love, a letter meant to be opened years from now.
Picture the person who might finish it, or simply be glad of it one day. If you pray, borrow the line from Hebrews, beholding them afar off; if not, just hold the face of whoever comes after you.

wordCard.voice: Cathedral. The church that holds a bishop's chair, sometimes raised by people who never saw it finished. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: built for grandchildren. Someone you'll never meet may stand under what you begin. See you tomorrow.
